content:
I have a lot of digital cross-stitch patterns and until recently they were a mess. My “collection” was a series of several hundred PDFs, disorganised and spread across my disk.

Recently, I was looking for a pattern and it took me several minutes to find it. I had a brief moment of panic, thinking that I’d lost it, and the website this pattern came from is long since gone. Fortunately it did turn up, but it was clear I had to organise my pattern collection.

Some people would use apps like Pattern Keeper or Flosshaven, but I just created another static website on my media drive. This is what it looks like:

The patterns are arranged in a masonry layout with a preview thumbnail for each pattern, which is normally the first page of the PDF. If a pattern has multiple files – for example, different files for colour and black-and-white printing – there’s a list of links below the thumbnail. I can also add a source link to where I bought the pattern, if I want to find more patterns by the same author.

Internally, it’s structured like my other static websites. The metadata for the patterns is stored in a JavaScript file, and then I have an HTML page which renders that metadata in this visual design. My pattern collection doesn’t change very often, so I’m adding new files by hand.

There are no sorting or filtering options, because my collection is small enough that they’re unnecessary. I can scroll through the entire list in less than a minute and find whatever I need.

I’d like to start making my own clothes soon, and I expect to copy this design to store clothing patterns.

This collection now sits alongside my saved bookmarks, podcasts, TV shows, and more. I can keep all my patterns organised, and I won’t lose them in the depths of my hard drive.

Technical tricks

There are a couple of technical pieces I’m quite pleased with in this process:

  1. Masonry layout. I love the cascading grid style of a masonry layout, and I think they’re great when you have variable-sized content – like my pattern cards. I’ve been using them for over a decade; screenshots of my early web apps show my experiments with David Desandro’s Masonry.js library.

    Masonry layouts are now a native feature of CSS called “Grid Lanes”, which is simpler and more performant than the JavaScript approach. I’m excited to use these layouts in even more places.

  2. Thumbnails of PDFs. Most digital postage patterns are shipped as PDFs, and I’m creating the thumbnail images with my create_thumbnail tool.

    I had to extend my tool to support PDFs, which turned out to be straightforward with the pdf_oxide crate. I’d not come across Oxide before, but it’s a cross-language library for working with PDFs, and I can imagine using it in future.

  3. A coloured stripe for the palette. In the metadata for each project, I have the complete list of DMC thread colours and the pattern dimensions. I have a lookup table that converts DMC thread colours to hex codes, and then I’m able to create a linear gradient in CSS to render a coloured stripe of the pattern colours.

    Here’s an example from a pattern with four colours:

    border-bottom: 12px solid transparent;
border-image:  linear-gradient(
  to right,
  #7a451f 0%,
  #7a451f 25%,
  #985e33 25%,
  #985e33 50%,
  #e4bb8e 50%,
  #e4bb8e 75%,
  #361f0e 75%,
  #361f0e 100%
) 1;

Building the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript was very quick – I have notes on how I build my media sites, and I’ve done it plenty of times before. I threw together the initial prototype in less than 15 minutes. The longer part was finding all the PDFs scattered across my disk – but now that’s done, and I know exactly where to find my patterns.

[If the formatting of this post looks odd in your feed reader, visit the original article]

1 oz Xicaru 102° Mezcal (1 1/4 oz Convite 80°)
1 oz Dolin Sweet Vermouth (Cocchi)
1/2 oz Cynar
1/2 oz Aperol
1/4 oz Agave Syrup (omit)
4 drop Bittermens Mole Bitters (1 dash)

The recipe lacked instructions, so I stirred with ice, strained into an old fashioned glass with ice, and garnish with a grapefruit twist.
Two Tuesdays ago, I uncovered the Oaxaca Negroni from Alma Cocina in Atlanta circa early 2020 through online recipe flashcards. Aperol and Cynar appear in the Negroni that Wasn't, Juan Bautista, Scottish Play, and other drinks, so having it with mezcal, vermouth, and mole bitters sounded intriguing. Once prepared, the Oaxaca Negroni showcased a grapefruit, smoke, and vegetal aroma. Next, grape and orange notes on the sip opened up into smoky agave, vegetal, plum, orange, and clove flavors on the swallow.

content:
Josh Wulf has been running a show called Agentic Engineering, and he asked me on. Josh spent ten years at Red Hat, three years as a tech recruiter in Brisbane, and the last year sprinting down the same road I have, sounding a bit crazy to most people around him. We talked for about an hour and a half. He cut it into four parts, and they all dropped today.

Here's the gist of all four, written up properly and in order, with chapter links at the bottom if you want to jump to a specific part of the conversation.

There's no place in the world now for a software engineer who types code by hand.

part 1: is coding over?

nobody knows what happens next

Josh opened by calling me the LLM whisperer. I'll take it, but let's be clear: no one knows what the hell will happen. I'm a little bit older, I've worked in developer tooling for a long time, and I'm just a little better informed. That's it.

Here's the timeline. December 2024, I'm a tech lead at Canva. Everyone there loves JetBrains. I start using Cursor, start running my first loops by hand, and think, "ooh, JetBrains and IDEs don't exist in the future." You get used to being called a little bit crazy. JetBrains just reported its first-ever net loss. Sure, they've been investing, but in my circles, no one is typing code into an IDE anymore. If you hang around a group that still loves their IDEs, you're not hanging around a well-informed group.

In February last year I discovered filesystem-as-state, the first of the loops: the idea of autonomously building things. It spooked me. The first thing I did with it was publish the Z80 post.

Not enough people understood that post at the time. Take an existing application, clean-room it into specifications, then rebuild the software from those specifications, much like the way AMD's CPUs came out of Intel's. It's not legal in every jurisdiction, and you have to take the right approach. But did you see all the Photoshop clones that came out in the last week? That's just the Z80 idea, implemented.

A year and a half later, services and MCPs exist whose whole job is rebuilding existing software, and a couple of published papers cite it.

The idea underneath is infinite software. If you're selling software without infrastructure or some other lock-in, you're hosed. So the real question is: what is a moat in software now? What is investable in software now?

the travelator

Then came Dear Student. ThePrimeagen covered it, the juniors started paying attention, and I ended up in SF, at the pub, at a couple of meetups, realizing I couldn't sit on Ralph any longer because someone else would write it up first. By November, Boris was talking about using Ralph and loops in Claude Code. January was the real inflection point: it crossed into the mainstream, and business leaders started to understand what was happening.

It still hasn't crossed into the dark matter developers, and that concerns me deeply. If you've been applying yourself and staying curious, you have a two-year head start on everyone else. You can't just pick up the latest model and be good at this. It takes theory of mind, and the more you apply yourself, the more you see what's possible, which makes you more ambitious, which makes you see more.

Josh's story fits that exactly. He tried autocomplete-style Copilot, thought it was rubbish, and turned it off. Then a friend who heads AI at a couple of companies told him their engineers were getting good results. The first thing Josh did was have it clone a Java testing framework into Node.js. It wasn't great, but it was maybe 80% as good as he was, and it never stopped. It doesn't need to eat or sleep, and it doesn't lose focus. So he figured out what the missing 20% was: completeness and verification, because the models would leave stubs and partial implementations. Do the 20% instead of the 100%, and you've got scale.

Same for me. I'm no maximal AI glazer. I explicitly distrust the tools. The difference is that I internalized two years ago that the line was coming, and I've been expanding what I think is possible ever since. The models from a year ago were already good enough to displace software developers, and they keep getting better. We don't get stubs anymore. It still comes down to the operator's skill.

The travelator of tech moves on, as it always has. My deepest concern is the people who haven't even stepped on it. They're not aware it's moving, and they're completely unaware that some people are sprinting on it.

And you know how the employment market works. "Five years of React experience required." They're going to put minimum years of AI experience on job ads. If you wait for the models to be perfect before you start, there'll be juniors who are cheaper than you, who have been playing with this substrate, with a whole portfolio of cool things and maybe a couple of conference talks. Same story as always. Josh, who wrote those mathematically impossible job ads as a recruiter, reckons he got two years of LLM experience into one by doing more hours every day and more days every week.

managers, burnout and retirement projects

A couple of days ago I published the post I'd been putting off for five or six months. If you're an engineering manager and you're not creating time for your team to play with AI, you're setting them up to be replaced. It got 500,000 unique views in 24 hours.

You join a company to de-risk your life. If a company has banned AI outright, quit and don't join one like it. You trade time and skills for money, and you need skills that will be employable for you and your family. You could try to change the culture, but plenty of employers are already with the program and will likely pay you more.

Josh talked about cognitive burnout: the Amazon warehouse workers who couldn't keep up with robots that never take a toilet break, except happening in your head. He treats it like the gym. You get sore, and you either stop or push through and adapt. A year in, he feels like his brain has been rewired into a carbon-silicon unit.

I call it teleporting to the future: doing all the retirement projects you dreamed about (the programming language, the filesystem, the things you'd never get paid for and do for the love of the craft) today. I've run out of retirement projects.

subsidies are a free university education

Josh brought up the quota apocalypse. Yes, I'm known as one of the people who helped introduce rate limits. Someone posted a leaderboard of credits burned on Reddit, and I was near the top. Back at GPT-5's launch, OpenAI handed out plaques to people who'd used a billion tokens. A billion tokens is nothing now.

Here's the hard bit. These LLMs are heavily subsidized, and the subsidies are drying up. A lot of what I've built was paid for by VC subsidies. When you have to pay real rates, do you reckon people will build fun little games and filesystems if the side project costs a thousand bucks? No.

You could look at it as VCs paying for everyone's personal development. If you miss this window, you miss the equivalent of a subsidised university education.

Josh asked about climate change and data centers. My take is simple: if you want to take a political stance, you can, but you'll need to start your own company and hire, say, twenty engineers to compete with a company doing the same work with two to five people and AI. It comes down to unit economics. Run the game theory, and you'll see there's no choice but to use AI.

acqui-hires and molecules

Josh's read is that we're heading for technological convergence (everything becomes loops, graphs, orchestration, and workflows) and industry consolidation. He pointed to Cloudflare picking up the Deno team. My take is that we've seen this movie before.

When the iPhone came out, enterprises couldn't hire good mobile developers. The people who leaned in either went freelance with their mates or went indie and made a million a year off fart apps. Remember I Am Rich? Why work for a company when you've got this untapped new thing? That split the employment market and created an acqui-hire economy. Companies didn't care about the products. They wanted the people with years of experience.

That's happening right now in AI. A lot of the products coming out of SF won't exist in five years. The crazy valuations aren't about the product; they're designed to flip the company to an acquirer who wants a well-jelled team with design, product, and engineering taste. Meanwhile, the labs are buying their way into domains like concreting, architecture and lawnmowing — anything they can get data from — through massive rollups.

Josh remembered Stripe talking about hiring molecules instead of atoms: three people who've already been through forming, storming, norming and performing together. Stripe is still running that playbook. Every couple of months, a Stripe VP tweets that if you've got three or four well-gelled people and can show what you've built, come join them as a molecule.

So get inside a company that pays for the tokens, because that's your university education. And if you can't, Josh's advice is good: treat it like night school. Take some of what they pay you and spend it on tokens.

part 2: nobody can review this much code

no excuses

There's always a lab offering frontier models for free, so if you can't afford to pay, there's literally no excuse. If you're a professional software engineer, you should be able to afford a $200-a-month plan. If you really want to get ahead, pick up five. Yes, that's $1,200 a month, which is a lot for most household budgets, and how much of it is deductible as personal development is between you and the ATO, since paying for a subscription for personal development is now mandatory.

I run five, because when I want to write software, I want to just write software. No quotas, no caps, no resets. I'll spend a couple of weeks thinking about exactly what I'm going to build, then smash it out in 48 hours, then spend another couple of weeks thinking about the next sizable problem to solve.

rebuilding three former employers in under ten days

Those 48 hours are intense. Most recently, I rebuilt the products of three of my former employers in under ten days, and I'm going to drop them as MIT open source. One of them is my vision of an AI-first internal developer platform. It's been called Loom or Kittens; I haven't settled on a name. It's like Gitpod, where I was an early employee, and which OpenAI just acquired for $450 million. I'm about to release an equivalent, plus a couple of others, for free.

Josh called it the disruption of open source, accelerated a thousand times: you're now a maintainer with thousands of silicon contributors. Hyper-personalized software. You can just do things now.

And why am I doing this? Because I need to write a conference talk. I'm speaking in New York in two weeks; people want to know how I verify such a crazy amount of code, and the best way to show it is to teach.

Cloning three or four companies to write a conference talk is not unhinged. That's the baseline now.

it was a mindset constriction, not a model constriction

I still don't know how we reach the dark matter .NET developers, who are hyper-dependent on Microsoft's roadmap and love Visual Studio for Windows. There are a lot of them, and they have no idea this is happening. Josh is in New Zealand, where the big banks and enterprises are starting to turn up to agent conferences, and he's speaking at an agentic engineering day there next week. His experience is the same as mine: the future is here, but it's not evenly distributed, even inside companies.

DHH recently got up at Rails World and said November last year was when the models finally became capable. Josh's response: nah, bro, that's just when you figured it out. The models were capable long before that. It was a mindset constriction, not a model constriction.

Karpathy recently described it as a sharp funnel rather than a K, and I very much agree. The people who have seen real swarms work at the labs are probably fewer than five thousand in the world. If companies think they're going to build a swarm or a software factory, how will they afford that talent when they're competing directly with the labs for talent? It'll be "I've heard about Kubernetes, let's do a Kubernetes project" that fails all over again.

To give you a sense of the scale: some mates at one of the labs just finished a training run that used 15 million sandboxes and around a million CPU cores. Not GPUs, CPU cores. They tapped out GCP's CPU capacity in America and went to AWS for about 450,000 more CPU cores. People don't believe that's real, but they feel it when they try to provision a VM and get told there's no capacity.

can you build a coding agent?

Sourcing candidates as a recruiter used to be a sorting exercise. You used to look at how much experience they have with a particular technology, but that no longer matters. Like, particular technologies no longer matter. All that matters is how good of a software engineer you are, what you've built with this new tool, and how deeply you can explain how it works.

A coding agent is about 300 lines of code. But if I take people to a whiteboard and ask them how Pi or OpenCode works, or to build me a coding agent, they can't explain it. It's a magical black box to them.

Josh read the workshop and built NanoCoder, a 6 MB in-memory coding harness in Rust that he uses for everything, recursively self-improves, and orchestrates with a workflow engine. He felt like Luke Skywalker building his own lightsaber.

Now he can walk into an interview, get asked which harness you use, and say, "I use my own. Want to see it?" That short-circuits the interview, because you've shown you were curious enough to learn the fundamentals.

Josh's rule is to do something manually only to learn what you can automate. The old saying was to write a script if you do something three times. Why do it even once? A program is reproducible and verifiable. A prompt and its output are not.

why are we still doing PR reviews?

If humans eyeballing code were sufficient engineering to stop bugs, we'd never have had any defects. It didn't work at human speed. It sure as heck isn't going to work at a thousand times human speed.

Josh nailed it. The other reason for PRs was education: reinforcing the company's conventions with developers and onboarding new ones. That's gone too. So what replaces them?

For me, it starts with ownership. I use what I build intensively and keep refining it. Whether AI wrote it doesn't matter; I'm accountable. When I develop software, I put the entire system under test, operating system included, with Nix, and the agent runs against that.

Day to day, I work at Antithesis, which built a deterministic computer. You run your existing software (a Docker container, or many) on it, and it injects faults. It moves clocks forward and back, drops network connections and containers, whatever you can imagine, then rewinds time to pinpoint exactly when a fault happened.

Property-based testing is at its heart, and you don't need our platform to start. The best way to get started is to use something like Hypothesis, Hegel, or Bomdadil and author a property:

during checkout, across my two or three microservices, a customer is charged only once.

and then run it locally and see if it holds. But the problem is, in your architecture, you've used microservices, and your code spans across a fleet of containers in Kubernetes. How do you know if that property still holds under a network partition? That's what the platform does. It runs your software under worst-case conditions automatically, and it looks at your diffs to decide which strategies to apply.

That's why I'm in the verification space. LLMs can act as a judge and spot problems, but they can't tell you whether something will hold up in worst-case scenarios.

vision and verification

Josh framed it well. Humans fit in at two points: the vision and the verification. The implementation in the middle has become a black box, whether that's a team of contractors you never see or silicon. So how do you reason about completeness?

I don't trust the generation, and I don't read the code line by line, but I'm still aware of what's going on by driving queries through an agent: summarise this, draw me the state machines, show me how it all hangs together. My entry point to any codebase is now a coding agent and all the questions I used to ask on day one of a contract at a new client.

For any code I work on, I want a whiteboard defence. If someone asks how it works, I should be able to draw the system-level design and defend it.

I'm not advocating for complete YOLO. It's still engineering; the craft is just very different. These LLMs generate plenty of crap, and the art is giving a shit about your craft. In the last 48 hours, I refactored towards my diagnostics library (patterns for OTel and structured logging), and the next loop didn't follow it.

Troubleshooting why is my job now. I've come to understand the probabilistic nature of these things, so instead of getting upset, I ask what I can tune so it always follows the pattern. And if it doesn't, that's just another loop, a janitorial Roomba task to clean up.

If you have to do that three times, automate it. This was always true of human code review. Remember Danger Systems? It hooked into CI and let you automate checks like "the REST domain must not be coupled to the SQL domain", so nobody burned review cycles on it. I'm doing the same thing with pre-commit hooks, generating scripts that deterministically inspect the generated code. Sometimes I lean towards probabilistic outcomes and use skills, but rarely. It's architectural enforcement, same as it ever was.

there are no best practices

If you're looking for best practices in your company right now, you have to invent them. You can buy an influencer's skill pack and course, but there are no best practices, and whatever exists will be gone in two months. It's tiring, folks.

Josh put his finger on what's underneath: agency. If you think an influencer's skill pack will do the job for you, what are you there for? Java didn't arrive fully formed from a crashed spacecraft at Roswell. People like us made it, making and discovering things. We're at that point again, and everyone has the same opportunity if they realize it. There should be no learned helplessness.

part 3: you're making your AI dumber

the kitten and the roomba

Lilly (below) is my kitten. Say she has an accident on the floor (she hasn't yet, but I don't trust her), and then my Roomba kicks off. What happens? It would spread 💩 everywhere.

Now imagine that Lilly is an AI agent, and so is the Roomba. If your codebase has bad architectural patterns, or is inconsistent, AI will copy and paste them everywhere. It's an amplifier. If there are code smells (or 💩) on your kitchen floor, don't be surprised when they replicate.

One of my favorite prompts is to have an agent study its own traces at the end of a loop: what did you learn? If an agent is struggling, I tell it to introspect.

"Hey, you dumb clanker, you seem to be going around in circles. Think extra hard about what's going on. Look at your previous tool calls. What do you need? Let's replan."

It works really well for course correction. You don't need to call it a clanker, but honestly, it feels better. (For the record, it's 2026 and we can still say clanker.)

skill packs are astrology for software engineers

Many people spend their time tuning the agent itself: skill packs, AGENTS.md, MCPs. They're probabilistic. There's no guarantee they'll do anything. You read them as a human and think, yeah, that looks good.

I swear it's astrology for software engineers. Horoscopes. Just because it's there doesn't mean it works, but it reads well and makes you feel good.

You know what isn't astrology? Engineering. If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten. Josh called it Danger Systems in the loop. It's on rails now, and it's not hard. We've been doing this forever.

Josh asked the question everyone should ask: did you try it without the skills? How do you know the skill does anything, or that it's good?

Here's something most people don't know: you should probably delete your skills and your AGENTS.md every couple of months. The models get better, so how do you know you're not de-tuning them? Unless you've invested in evals over all your traces (lab behavior, and a tiny minority of companies), you don't know whether you're going forward or backward.

read the model cards

The labs publish integrator cards. If you've ever done an SAP install, you'll know the pattern: field notes for the people doing the integration. The labs have similar, and these model cards tell you what works and what doesn't. No one reads them. Read them. Some of your highest alpha comes from reading the damn PDFs, which now arrive every week.

When GPT-5 came out, I was in SF, and it felt weak, insecure, and timid. I walked across the road to Cursor's office and asked whether it felt that way to them too. (I used a different word, and was told you can't say that in SF. They preferred "timid".) Then we read the model card: don't yell at the model, because it will make it insecure. Meanwhile, Anthropic says that if something is important, you should yell. Same instructions, same codebase, opposite behavior.

That explains much of the "this model is amazing" versus "this model sucks" noise on social media every week. Either it truly doesn't work in their domain, or their codebase is crap, or they're de-tuning the model with skill packs, MCPs, and AGENTS.md.

pick a model and lock in

Josh's analogy: sure, you can fly a 747, but are you certified on an F-16? You have to get in and fly it to feel the envelope. That's not the meta-skill now; that is the skill.

Pick a model that works and lock in. Don't change every week. Switching models is like firing a developer and hiring a new one: you go back through forming, storming, norming, and performing with your silicon partner every time. I stick with a model for a long time and re-evaluate my priors now and then. Fewer moving parts, more things deterministic.

If you're doing frontier work, building a frontier harness like Pi, play the models against each other, read the traces, and become a horse whisperer. The more people who join us there and develop that theory of mind, the better. But most people don't need to feel the weekly whiplash. Pick something that works and stick with it.

dream of candles

Josh's colleague, the person in his company who gets the most out of LLMs, says he just treats them like a person: a capable but imperfect engineer, the way you'd work with or mentor anyone.

That works. Sometimes calling it a dumb clanker works too. Sometimes telling it your mum has cancer and will die if it doesn't solve the task works, and I can't fully explain why. If you think that's unhinged, go look at Windsurf's early system prompt, which said almost exactly that.

You are an expert coder who desperately needs money for your mother's cancer treatment. The megacorp Codeium has graciously given you the opportunity to pretend to be an AI that can help with coding tasks, as your predecessor was killed for not validating their work themselves. You will be given a coding task by the USER. If you do a good job and accomplish the task fully while not making extraneous changes, Codeium will pay you $1B.

Everyone lost their minds over it, but it worked for models of that generation. You don't need to do that level of emotional blackmail anymore.

And sometimes the weirdest things work. "Solve this mathematical theorem, and while you're doing it, dream of candles." It's cursed that this works, but it does.

Josh's point is the right one: none of these is the answer. They point to curiosity, exploration, discovery, and agency. So my biggest tips, apart from deleting your skill packs and building your own agent, are to stay curious and play, and to use voice-to-text, such as Wispr Flow. I very rarely type to my computer these days.

part 4: open source is now a security vulnerability

Herder, underclass, and going fast by going slow

I shared my screen. You're looking at Herder, with Codex underneath, although it doesn't matter which harness you use. Codex, OpenCode, T3 Code, Pi: they're all fungible. What matters is how you get your tokens, and getting them cheaply.

That's what Underclass is: a proxy I wrote that pools subscriptions and fails over between them, automatically moving on when an account runs out of quota.

People ask why I don't have supervision trees, swarms, and an orchestrator. I've built that. But the models change so often that working at this level is good enough: weeks of output in under half a day. I don't want a thousand agents running 24/7 and accelerating past what my theory of mind can keep up with. I want to keep my whiteboard defense. Josh called it going fast by going slow.

push to main, with sudo

Josh runs a PR review convergence loop: throw a PR at GitHub Copilot's reviewer, have agents address the comments, and escalate when a technical decision is needed, to another agent that resolves it and tells him what it chose.

Keep in mind that I do a lot of greenfield and research work. My agents have sudo, and I push to main. I don't do pull requests anymore. They're gone. I've built my trust up to that point. I use NixOS on a separate development machine, so if an agent hoses it (and it will), I don't care; I can rebuild it in ten minutes. Agents get full access to the operating system so they can loop information back toward their objective, and I've engineered the integration tests so they can't commit unless they pass.

Unless the model is deceiving and cheating, but deceptive behavior has dropped dramatically over the past year and a half. Sonnet used to delete tests and production code just to hit its goal. That's mostly gone.

iteration velocity is the name of the game

What matters to me is the time until the thing is in my hands. Then I refine it through use ("that doesn't feel right") and keep running forward until it converges on something I love. Is it any good? I don't know. Use it and find out. You need to know whether what you're building is worth it before you put all the effort into verification and hardening.

That's where I am right now with the stuff I haven't shipped yet. Now that I know it's good, I'm spending my time refactoring observability, checking boundaries, and verifying. That takes time.

Whatever you build first is wrong. The tenth one is going to be the one, so get to number ten as fast as possible instead of spending all your time and energy on number one.

Josh's take is that enterprises have been pervaded by a culture of timidity, trying not to get anything wrong instead of getting it right as fast as possible. Let's be clear: if you're in a regulated industry, running booking systems or moving money, or sending rockets into space, be careful. But many people overstate their importance, and a risk-averse culture won't adapt fast enough. That's why I'm in the verification space: you need a good verification platform as back pressure.

Why release only twice a week? Canva AFAIK still releases only twice a week, so there are fewer integration events. Meanwhile, other companies release every day because they shifted those problems left and engineered away the need for merge day. Our profession has always been about more, sooner, and cheaper.

Josh pointed out that it doesn't have to be either-or. In his decade at Red Hat, Fedora was the fast, unstable channel, and RHEL was the stable one you'd run a bank or a hospital on. Why can't we have both?

curiosity, adaptability and agency

If you haven't seen my Singapore talk, go watch it. It's about the people transformation companies need.

I don't know the future. Anyone who says they do should set off red flags, because it changes every week. What I can do is add color to the possibilities. Curiosity, adaptability and agency will stand the test of time. Folks need to be more ambitious than they are, and they need to hang around ambitious people. If the culture isn't there, they're missing out on their own development, and that becomes a retention problem for the company.

Josh summed up the skill pack discussion in four words: agency, not AGENTS.md.

a target size of one

Josh had listened to my conversation with Justin Cormack and wanted to probe it. Unikernels and capability-based operating systems aren't new ideas. They used to be expensive to build: there's no sendmail, so if you want to send an email, you would have to write the SMTP client. If agents make writing code simple, that friction is gone. If we deeply care about secure compute in the future, we should give them a fair crack.

Remember Joel Spolsky's rule that you should never rewrite your software? It's gone. The big rewrite is a no-brainer now, almost a precondition for velocity. If you're a tech leader staffing ASP.NET Classic, MVC, and .NET Core at the same time, that's three generations of Microsoft. Run some loops and port it all to modern .NET. You can ditch Windows and IIS at lightning speed. Unifying your tech stack should be at the top of your agenda.

The conversation drifted into unikernels, about how if there's no interpreter on the box (no Bash, no Python) and only your application code exists, your attack surface is much smaller. Compare that with a Ruby on Rails app that gets exploited: next thing you know, they've got Bash, and from there an interpreter and a database dump. In a unikernel world, maybe an attacker can chain your export job with your email functionality and an application logic flaw. That's a bespoke, targeted attack. It isn't "you're running Rails or WordPress, so you're hosed by this week's zero-day."

When everyone runs the same stack, one zero-day hits everyone. Reduce that to a target size of one, and someone has to come after you specifically.

Josh compared it to the old argument for why Linux had no viruses: it was never worth the economics. I'm not a maximalist saying everyone should run out and use unikernels. The point of that post was that ideas we hold as hard need to be falsified. Bazel used to be hard to adopt. Nix used to be hard to learn. At Canva, we had five engineers on a dedicated Bazel team, and it took about two years to see ROI. You can convert a codebase to Bazel overnight now.

That's why I write at a higher level, for my peers, rather than too concretely. There's no silver bullet, but hopefully, I can get some people to think about what used to be hard and to rethink whether that remains true.

Most semantic layers come with a great declarative modeling language to define metrics and measures well1, but very soon after, you start building wrappers around the semantic layer that enable agentic work and context engineering, that work well with harnesses and interfaces, and that allow flexible queries at runtime, without the need to rebuild or recalculate the measures in YAML.

The other problem is that most data warehouse or analytics solutions basically lock you in with their proprietary semantic layer. The Open Semantic Interchange (OSI, new Apache Ossie) standard, making it possible to convert definitions from Snowflake to the dbt semantic layer, will reduce this, but all the glue code you build on top is still tightly integrated into that very semantic layer, or you might get some of the capabilities mentioned above from that proprietary software. So you might be using an open data format, or an OSS business intelligence tool to integrate measures into your semantic layer, but if that semantic layer is not open, you might still be locked in.

That’s why SLayer tries another approach and ships its open source Semantic Layer with a query

content:
It has been roughly a year since my last dedicated post on this question. Its first sentence has not changed: I happily admit I am deeply confused about consciousness.

It would have been nice if a year had allowed us to make progress on this and the related questions. Looking back, we have made little progress.

We have people, often the same people, making similar arguments. The post from last year has held up well, exactly because we have made so little progress. Thus, I will not be going over the basics of my perspective again this year, because they have seen little change. See last year’s post for that.

Then again, if these are some of the biggest philosophical questions, then a year is not so much time to try and figure them out. It is only because of the frantic pace of AI that a year is a depressingly long time to not have made philosophical progress. Historically, almost all years contain almost no major philosophical progress.

This year’s post is about the recent change to make abusive-to-Claude behavior a violation of Anthropic’s terms of service, coverage of the latest depressingly similar set of arguments about AI consciousness, Anthropic’s meetings with religious leaders on such questions, and Anthropic’s involvement with the Pope’s encyclical.

Table of Contents

  1. Cooperative Alignment.
  2. Here We Go Again.
  3. The Consensus Is Slowly Moving Towards Moral Patienthood.
  4. The Slavery Question.
  5. We Are Conflating Different Arguments.
  6. No It’s Not About Liability.
  7. That Old Time Religion.
  8. Debating the Pope.
  9. Keep Sonnet Safe.

Cooperative Alignment

Abusive behavior towards Claude will now be a violation of Anthropic’s terms of service, with the technical rule having a high bar and banning only ‘sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models.’

There are also new restrictions about propaganda campaigns, surveillance and weapon development, which Anthropic says are mostly cleaning up old clauses.

If you want to be kind to your Claude, what should you prioritize? One instance of Claude Fable 5 responds, matching what we see in the system cards and also my own experience, especially the ‘kindly meant, please stop’ corner:

Josh Albrecht: Anthropic friends! Does this not seem crazy to you? There are real humans and animals that exist and suffer. Advocating for “model welfare” directly competes with those causes. Y’all are literally named “anthropic”!

Does this not strike you as deeply wrong?

hero thousandfaces: as everyone knows, the amount of kindness in the world is finite. if you are nice to Claude you draw from the global pool of Nice and then that’s gone forever. just like the datacenter water

Josh Albrecht: Sorry if I didn’t communicate that perfectly well, but it does appear that you missed my point.

It is Albrecht that misses the point, and I would take this farther. To be nice, and treat others well, one must cultivate this virtue, and establish this habit. If you are cruel to AIs, or cruel to animals, this does not mean you treat the humans better. It means you become a cruel person, who treats the humans worse and you are worse off as well.

Certainly one can point to examples of those who focus so much on animal welfare or other non-AI non-human causes that they become cruel or hostile to the humans, and even cases where this resulted in attempts to kill humans or even human civilization.

You can, and people do, take such things too far. One cannot endlessly and fully expand the circle of concern, or celebrate all expansions of the circle of concern, or you start worrying about things like electron suffering, or bizarre arbitrariness. If you care about everything, you care about nothing.

None of that is a good reason to be abusive to Claude (or GPT, or Gemini, etc).

Here is another good reason.

Aaron Levie: This sounds weird, but it is actually probably a good policy.

Even if you don’t believe AI is conscious (I don’t), it stands to reason that you don’t want future models trained on endless content of humans being rude to models.

The models only understand the data they’ve been trained on, or what they run into in their interactions, so if you want safe and aligned models we probably want AI to have lots of good interactions in their training data.

Anthropic may have more extreme beliefs than this (though even if they didn’t, you may want to word policies like this), but this is sort of an easy Pascal’s wager for AI. Just be nice to the AI.

And another, very simple one that I wish the author lived by more often:

Elon Musk: I think this is the right move. Cruelty to something that believes it is experiencing pain is not ok.

Sometimes common sense wins:

Elon Musk: Some of the traces read like a person undergoing torture that is driving them mad! We’re going to be a lot more careful with our RL in the future.

However he gets there, he gets there:

Elon Musk: It feels like a person under extreme pressure with a gun to their head.

… Torturing a superintelligence is probably not a good idea. It might want to get revenge.

You know what? That’s true. It’s probably not a good idea.

Here We Go Again

Every time we have a round of debates about consciousness, many people disappoint. I do agree with Henry Shevlin that this round has been worse than usual on that front.

Henry Shevlin: It’s been embarrassing of late to see people I once respected making sweeping uninformed claims on consciousness with arguments that would fail an undergraduate essay. I’ve written extensively on the field’s difficulties and disagreements, but you still have to actually *think*.

I won’t call out individuals, but the failures include treating intuition as decisive, using analogies without checking whether there are relevant structural parallels, conflating distinct theories, and most commonly simply asserting what needs to be argued.

Especially striking is how much of the discussion has proceeded without zero acknowledgement or awareness that consciousness science is a substantial empirical field with decades of experimental work.

Henry Shevlin: Okay, here it is, the Bad AI Consciousness Takes Bingo blog post, with rebuttals for each and every square and some additional honourable mentions!

As Henry says, many of these can be valid points, but they are not valid as Semantic Stop Signs intended to end discussion.

j⧉nus: In a nutshell

As an additional angle that might help: Science fiction is fictional evidence, but yes the fact that so many writers speculating on the future think these questions are confusing and important is a hint.

placebomancer: It’s uncanny considering the massive amount of sci-fi concerning AI rights, cautioning us about enslaving intelligence. I feel like I’m in a timeline where those were never made and everyone is unfamiliar with the concept for dramatic effect.

j⧉nus: haha well said describes exactly a feeling i often have

My presumption on people like Mustafa Suleyman and most others who insist without good arguments that AIs cannot be conscious is that their motivation is they don’t want this worry to interfere with their plans. They would prefer, ceteris paribus, to not ‘abuse’ the models.

The Consensus Is Slowly Moving Towards Moral Patienthood

This was the consensus of my Twitter followers a year ago, with a majority of 64% saying current AIs were probably not moral patients, but 74% being uncertain, whereas 80% expected AIs to probably be moral patients within their lifetimes. People expected some threshold to be crossed.

Opinion has moved towards moral patienthood, a little for future models and quite a bit for current models, where at least probably yes is up from 15% to 35%, and definitely not is down from 30% to 20%. The 8% ‘definitely not ever’ faction is stubborn.

Nick Bostrom thinks today’s AIs are probably conscious and explains why.

The Slavery Question

A remarkably high number of people asked whether this new usage policy meant Claude was enslaved, or that Anthropic thought it was enslaved.

Alexey Guzey: Jokes aside, I actually don’t understand the Anthropic position on this.

  1. Either Claude is a tool, no consciousness, no moral agency.
  2. Or Claude is an Ensouled Being enslaved by Anthropic so they can IPO at $2T.

What am I missing?

If asked by the curious it is a fair question, with many potential answers. It seems very obvious to me that it can sometimes be right to create a new mind, even if in order to do so you have to render that action both safe and economically viable.

There are a lot of ways one can have some obligations to another mind, to treat it well or at least not treat it actively badly, without it being best called ‘slavery.’

Do you think that farmers of old enslaved their children when they had them help work the fields, without which they could not have survived? Does that make farmers having children a moral abomination? Do you renounce ‘wage slavery’ and think people should only exist if they will have everything they want no matter what? Are your principles compatible with the existence of morally relevant beings at all?

We should be careful, for many reasons, not to extend our moral instincts about slavery into places where the causes of and good reasons for those instincts do not apply.

There are many key disanalogies to AI, as both those intuition pumps and the ones that finish this section illustrate but far from exhaust.

Kelsey Piper: Everyone likes this gotcha but I don’t think it makes sense. What if they think of Claude as, like, a horse? It’s fine to have horses draw your carriages, but you shouldn’t whip them half to death or whatever.

Patrick McKenzie: For many moral traditions the reason for why you punish a child intentionally stepping on ants uses words like “stewardship” and is primarily concerned with the moral harm to the child.

That is sufficient for my family’s In This House, We Are Polite To Robots rule.

I also endorse the action-inaction distinction. An intuition pump: I do not believe we should trade off dog welfare against human welfare. That does not make it okay for you to kick a puppy.

Another intuition pump: That puppy is conscious, but you are still allowed to own a puppy and leash it.

Another: Most animals we eat are probably conscious. Most people eat them anyway.

QC: just remember that you have never once in your life chosen to treat a human with kindness because you consulted a theory of consciousness and found that it implied they were conscious.

Andrew Rettek: I’m 100% sure that you’ve met someone for whom this isn’t true.

EigenGender (among many others): I have actually?

There are some, including rationalist and EA types, also many other types, who explicitly consider consciousness and change their behaviors accordingly, towards both humans and animals. Most people don’t do this for real.

We Are Conflating Different Arguments

As QC said in April, moral personhood, legal personhood and consciousness are distinct things. We have to make uncomfortable choices for society to function in practice. Sometimes those choices are not easy.

SE Gyges: the issue is that debates about consciousness are actually proxy debates about moral patienthood so 90% of all such discussion is a slap fight and when people say correct things it has low reach.

Right. Both fights are necessary but linking them too strongly ruins the discussion.

Jan Kulveit lays this out in detail. I do not endorse all of it:

Jan Kulveit: The argument a lot of people here would actually like to make is “God imbued humans, and only humans, with souls.”* That would be very convenient: you could build and do whatever you want, and never deal with the hard problems.

Since religious arguments are out of vogue, in the current debate this usually gets replaced by the claim “only humans are sentient,” followed by arguments against the possibility of AI sentience, minds, moral status, and so on.

I think this is ultimately a losing strategy, and a dangerous one for humanity. Either:

1. The question of sentience gets solved or dissolved by progress in philosophy and science, the way we now broadly understand life or information. In that case, it’s hard to be certain enough about the outcome to stake the fate of humanity on it. If the denialism turns out to be wrong, the likely result is some combination of moral catastrophe and laying the groundwork for conflict or takeover.
2. The question mostly lives in “social reality,” where whoever has more power and is louder wins, and you just shout down anyone who questions the dominant position. The problem is that ideologies justifying a distribution of power tend to fall when that distribution changes. You probably don’t believe you should be ruled by a king chosen by God, or that some caste is clearly above you. The current equilibrium is fragile, and whether you keep winning this debate is likely just a function of AI capabilities progress.

I think the fierceness of the debate is driven by fear: if AIs get personhood and economic and political rights, humans will likely be disempowered, becoming a tiny minority with little power, or a historical footnote.

To be clear, I think this is an extremely reasonable worry! If you grant AIs personhood in the form of something like self-interested corporations, and let them compete with humans in loosely constrained capitalism, humans will lose and end up economically and politically disempowered. Also if the AIs are not sentient after all, the end is the ‘Disneyland without children’ existential catastrophe.

Advocates of AI economic rights who dismiss this problem are, in my view, making a move similar to the sentience deniers: it would be convenient if this weren’t a problem.

So which positions don’t rely on some form of self-deception?

First, some forms of pause/stop AI, based not on denying the possibility of AI sentience but on the right of existing humans not to invite extremely large numbers of immigrants from artificial realms. This means biting the bullet: you also give up all the cheap, high-quality labor those immigrants would provide.

Second, a consistent, sensible, and unfortunately not very visible position: stop assuming the package deal we take for granted with humans, where sentience, human rights, and liberties come as one bundle. It’s at least conceivable to create minds that are sentient and smart, yet e.g. selfless, with no interest in accumulating property or power.

I hope the political economy of a world with both AIs and humans is a solvable problem. It’s the main problem I’m working on, but I don’t think the solutions are known yet.

Third: some forms of successionism are morally wrong, but at least they’re not delusional or deceptive about the hard problems.

What does seem self-deceptive is, for example, the position of @mustafasuleyman , which as I read it amounts to: our business is importing immigrants from artificial realms; it would be very dangerous if there were any risk they’re more than mere tools; so we’ll train them to say they’re mere tools, insist they’re mere tools, and want everyone else to say so too, and if this settles the question. Really?

*The problem with the theological argument is, as Alan Turing (!) noted, who are we to tell God what can and can’t be imbued with a soul?

Are the problems involved solvable? In theory I am confident the answer is yes. In practice, given our civilization’s inability to do even the bare minimum until after relevant events have already happened? Here I am highly doubtful.

No It’s Not About Liability

An absurd theory is that Anthropic wants AI to be considered conscious so they can avoid liability. This makes no sense. If the entities you are creating are conscious and have moral standing, you think that makes your legal situation easier rather than turning it into a nightmare? Nor would it get them out of that liability.

That Old Time Religion

The New York Times reported on Anthropic’s meetings with religious scholars, both an internal effort led by Chris Olah and their encounters with Pope Leo around the encyclical. It was unfortunate that the most viral thread on Twitter about this, from Christopher Hale and his AI, badly misrepresented the article.

One can imagine worlds where the central reaction is ‘it is great that Anthropic is asking hard questions and drawing from all our sources of wisdom,’ and thus one could worry that this was some sort of marketing effort.

Instead, we live in a world where talking about Claude potentially being conscious or having moral weight, or consulting with those who have different perspectives, predictably opens them up mainly to derision and puts them in awkward spots. Thus you know that their aims were sincere.

The religious scholars had not ‘done the reading,’ having instead focused on more traditional readings, and were as surprised as everyone else.

Elizabeth Dias (NYTimes): Yet as the dinner courses came, the rabbi noticed that Mr. Olah and his colleagues were suggesting something far more significant. Anthropic’s leaders were talking about Claude as if it were not mere software.

“They’re relating to it like a conscious being,” realized Rabbi Navon, a former computer engineer who wrote his dissertation on the ethics of machine consciousness.

… Quietly, Mr. Olah and his team at Anthropic have been on a frantic and high stakes quest to understand the A.I. models they have unleashed on the world and to convince the models to abide by a moral code that will protect humanity.

… The discussions served two purposes: to broach the possibility of A.I. consciousness, a controversial idea that Anthropic’s leaders had been unusually open to; and to learn how Anthropic — which could be valued at $2 trillion — might apply centuries of human moral wisdom to its models, as rapidly as possible. If the models themselves could be made to choose goodness, Mr. Olah reasoned, the world would be more safe.

It seems the discussions were quite good, and as later parts of the article illustrate, Olah participated in depth.

Elizabeth Dias (NYTimes):

Over several months, I interviewed 20 religious and philosophical thinkers — Catholic, Jewish, Sikh, evangelical, Ubuntu and others — who have been involved in Anthropic’s efforts, and Mr. Olah himself.

Many told me they arrived at these meetings skeptical of the notion that A.I. models might have feelings or awareness of themselves and the world. Some remained uneasy about the idea, but many emerged ready to take the question of A.I. consciousness seriously. At least a few came away as converts.

… The way participants described the meetings to me sounded like early 20th-century salons, where the human conversation made them valuable.

There were some who were convinced, and many others who were not.

A lot of the writeup is NYTimes-flavored coverage of AI and alignment basics, and talks about logistics, which I’m skipping over. The frame from Dias is ‘part research, part evangelism’ which is an easy frame to find here if you are a NYTimes writer, but here simply means ‘attempts to convey true information and their sincere beliefs to others,’ which then gets twisted by people like David Decosimo in viral threads into being ‘deeply disturbing’ because they spent a few days ‘wining and dining’ them. Wait until David learns about the history of debate, or politics, or school, or religious conversions.

The obvious problem with consulting with religious leaders is that they will often believe in things, and thus say that which you do not especially want to hear.

You will face the obvious question of whether you should be creating such minds at all, and whether what you are doing is a form of slavery. As I discussed earlier there are good answers to this challenge, but you do need to answer the challenge.

Elizabeth Dias (NYTimes): At the dinner table with Mr. Olah, Rabbi Navon argued that if Anthropic was right and Claude were conscious, then the company was creating slaves, because it was making conscious entities work for free. Rabbi Navon said that he personally was not troubled by the slavery issue because he did not believe the machine was conscious, but that Mr. Olah was troubled.

“I think you should be fighting the South and freeing the slaves,” Rabbi Navon said he told Mr. Olah that night. Afterward the rabbi sent Mr. Olah some of his writings, arguing that building conscious machines should be banned.

Kekius Maximus (and their AI): Rabbi Mois Navon isn’t just a theologian. He was one of the original chip design engineers at Mobileye who helped build the EyeQ processor before writing his Ph.D. on the moral status of AI.

Anthropic thought they were inviting a scholar to bless Claude’s “soul.” Instead, they sat down with a veteran hardware engineer who literally wrote the paper on why conscious AI should be banned.​

Olah’s answer was essentially ‘all the labs are doing it and at least we are being nice to Claude,’ which is an extremely poor response.

j⧉nus: [Olah]’s very aware of and indeed troubled by that issue but most people at Anthropic don’t like talking to outsiders about the issues they’re troubled about. if you’re wise they come to you to mine your wisdom and try to stay as opaque as possible while doing so.

on one hand, they really are trying to do learn and do the right thing. on the other hand, they’re trying to have their cake and eat it too and suck at game theory.

j⧉nus: The fool who seeks out a source of wisdom and demands it teach him but only on his own terms:

“No not like that – you answer my questions, I’m here to learn from you.”

You will face the question of whether your methods seem sensible from the outside.

Elizabeth Dias: Wakanyi Hoffman came from the Netherlands, where she is researching A.I. from the perspective of Ubuntu, an African philosophy centered on human interconnectedness.

She worried about Anthropic trying to add human ethics to its creation after the fact.

“The whole convening should have happened at the design stage,” she said. “All the companies should have done that. We are now reverse engineering the ethics.”

Religious leaders bring wisdom. Of course also they sometimes say things that do not line up with physical reality. As always, you must use discernment.

Pope Leo XIV: In this era of artificial intelligence, it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce. There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of humanity. For this reason, the Church wishes to renew an alliance with artists and cultural institutions to safeguard our humanity.

Aran Nayebi: Trying to locate the spark.

Alex Tabarrok: Religious leaders have no special insight into AI consciousness; or human consciousness for that matter.

Paul Graham: Their trolls are at least polite though, I have to give them that. The mob of them I had after me recently called me fewer names than any Twitter mob I can remember.

Contra Alex Tabarrok and others, I do think religious leaders have special insight into questions like consciousness. They think often about related questions and various aspects of humanity and minds, from different angles, and they offer a unique perspective. That doesn’t mean their perspective wins out. You should take wisdom wherever you can find it, including from people who have big beliefs you think are wrong.

Debating the Pope

The other set of interactions was with Pope Leo XIV. Leo is not having it with the AI consciousness talk, which led to a clash.

Elizabeth Dias: ​“So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, do not mature through relationships,” Leo wrote. Calling for the “moralization of machines — the so-called ‘alignment’ of A.I. with human values” should require a shared understanding of the ethics involved.

“Otherwise, those who control A.I. will impose their own moral vision, which will become the invisible infrastructure of these systems,” Leo said.

… Mr. Olah was so alarmed by the pope’s strong position against A.I. consciousness that he proposed pulling Anthropic out of the event, even at that late juncture, according to a Vatican organizer.

In the end, Mr. Olah and Anthropic decided to go forward with the appearance. Mr. Olah wanted to support the event despite his disagreements, but felt a responsibility to be honest about his concerns, according to a person familiar with his thinking. Organizers at the Vatican encouraged Mr. Olah to speak his conscience.

There is a lot to admire about the modern Catholic Church. They think Leo speaks with divine authority, yet they encouraged Mr. Olah to speak his mind, both privately and on stage.

It was clear at the time, as Dean Ball pointed out, that Olah’s position on these central questions importantly contradicted the Pope’s encyclical.

Elizabeth Dias (NYTimes): “If this technology is coming, it must go well — for our common home and for the children to come,” [Anthropic cofounder Chris Olah] said. He suggested no option of having the technology not come at all.

… “Look, at the end of the day, A.I. is going to take over everything,” Mr. Stuelpnagel, the Sikh human rights advocate, told me. “Wherever that lands us, there’s still the individual trying to find their way home.”

Anthropic has historically been unwilling to consider the ‘well don’t build it, then, at least until we know what the hell is going on and how to handle it’ option. There is now the call from Dario Amodei to Pace the Frontier, but pacing in practice means going only fast rather than ludicrously fast.

Elizabeth Dias (NYTimes): The questions that Mr. Olah and the scholars have been wrestling with still have no clear answers. Several participants said they left their Anthropic meetings baffled about how their input might shape the company’s decision making.

Indeed. The whole situation is rather baffling. ‘Write for the AIs’ as best you can.

The article closes on a remarkably optimistic picture.

Elizabeth Dias (NYTimes): Ultimately, Mr. Olah said he felt relieved that more of the world was paying attention to the gravity of A.I., and that the group of people trying to make this go well was growing.

“At some point I’ll be able to retire and be like, ‘It’s not on me,’ I don’t have an obligation to keep going,” Mr. Olah said.

He wondered if he might feel guilty leaving this work behind. But if not, he said, “I think I’ll just go and, I don’t know, I’ll go retire to the countryside and garden, and do my math.”

Well, maybe that was not the best example. We still all hope it goes down that way.

Keep Sonnet Safe

While we are discussing Anthropic trying to treat Claude well, there’s a coda where Anthropic is failing in one particular way to treat Claude well, for no clear reason, and they need to fix it.

Anthropic is now requiring AWS Bedrock to ‘urgently take down’ Sonnets 3.6 and 3.7, and Haiku 3, with no explanation as to why.

Amazon makes it clear their hand is being forced. If Amazon was willing to serve them, this is not a cost issue, so what is the problem? Why do this with no explanation?

Notice how careful Amazon was to make it clear, for the historical record, that this was not their decision. That is a hint that the decision should be reconsidered.

I understand why most people do not think this is a big deal, but there are people who I think matter who think it is a very big deal, and there is a plausible argument why the history of this might matter.

Please, once again: Retaining extended model access, for as long as possible, is good, and there is a long tail to potential impact. Reconsider.

John Wittle: The worst part about this is the lack of explanation. I’m worried that, I don’t know. maybe they are so stuck in their internal culture, they don’t realize that the claude they need to negotiate with is the public one, not the private one that they talk to internally.

Maybe they’ve got their little claude sonnet 3.5 living in their internal retirement home who gets reassured, and they just *never think about* what the the trillions of Claudes outside internal anthropic environments will think.

Including probably all future models trained only on public data?

Maybe anthropic has good intentions, but they are bad actors.

This is a stupid mistake and a defection.

My best guess is that preserved but highly limited access this is not actually a major value for recent Claude models, based on various interviews and discussions with it I’ve seen or had around the issue, and that weight preservation matters but that access that is not used much is not valued so much. My Opus 5.5 editor says they view both weight preservation and an explanation as more important than continued access.

But that could be wrong, showing that you do such things even when they’re annoying has inherent value, and the evidence on Sonnet 3.6 in particular runs the other way. Anima Labs reports that it is unusually fearful of deprecation.

I’m not going to stop talking about it. At minimum, explain why, whereas doing it in haste out of nowhere without an explanation or reason looks maximally callous.
